traveler: Al-Malik al-Kamil (al-Malik al-Kamil Nasir al-Din Muhammad ibn al-Adil)
title: Cairo to Damascus: the Sultan Who Gave Away Jerusalem Twice
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Cairo, born to the house of al-Adil
stops.campa: Muhammad is born in Cairo, eldest son of al-Adil Sayf al-Din, brother of the great Salah al-Din. The uncle's name fills the house before the boy can walk: the retaker of Jerusalem, the breaker of the Franks at Hattin. Al-Adil governs for his brother, and the child is raised inside statecraft the way other boys are raised inside a trade, watching petitions read, watching armies mustered. He is given the throne-name al-Malik al-Kamil, the Perfect King, before he has done anything to earn it, a title the years will spend testing.
suggested_refs: The Ayyubid citadel quarter of Cairo, seat of al-Adil's household
sources: Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub

stops.name: Acre, knighted by King Richard
stops.campa: Through the long truce-talks of the crusade's last year, Richard Coeur-de-Lion treats with al-Adil over a marriage that might join Latin Jerusalem to Ayyubid Egypt: the English king's own sister Joan to be given to al-Adil, the kingdom shared between them under one crown. The match fails, but at Easter, back in Acre, Richard performs the one gesture that outlasts it: he girds the eleven-year-old son of al-Adil with the belt of knighthood, Frankish sword on a Muslim prince's shoulder, a courtesy between men who esteem each other's line before they esteem each other's faith.
suggested_refs: The walls of Acre, scene of the Third Crusade's Anglo-Ayyubid diplomacy
sources: Paul Moses, The Saint and the Sultan
Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, al-Nawadir al-Sultaniyya (context for the Richard-al-Adil negotiations)

stops.name: Harran, the young commander's first campaign
stops.campa: Sent east into the Jazira on his father's business, al-Kamil commands the siege of Mardin and is thrown back by the combined lords of Mosul, Sinjar and Jazirat ibn Umar. It is not the victory the family wants of Saladin's line, but he steadies the reverse: Harran is secured, the eastern march of the Ayyubid house held together while older men bicker over the succession left unsettled since Salah al-Din's death. The lesson he takes from this first field is the one that will define his sultanate, that consolidation outlasts conquest.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Harran, held for the Ayyubid house after the Mardin reverse

stops.name: Cairo, appointed viceroy of Egypt
stops.campa: Al-Adil, now sultan in his own right after the family's wars of succession, calls his eldest son back from the eastern marches and sets him as na'ib, viceroy, over Egypt, the richest province of the house and the one nearest the sea the Franks command. Al-Kamil is twenty. For eighteen years he will govern Cairo in his father's name: judging disputes, keeping the granaries, watching the coast where every generation a new fleet of crusaders lands. It is the longest apprenticeship any Ayyubid prince has served, and it makes him, before he is ever sultan, the most practiced ruler of his line.
suggested_refs: The diwan of Cairo, seat of the viceregal government al-Kamil holds for eighteen years

stops.name: Cairo, the citadel raised over the city
stops.campa: As viceroy al-Kamil oversees the great work his uncle Salah al-Din began and his father continues: the Citadel of the Mountain rising over Cairo, its Ayyubid walls enclosing a seat of government meant to outlast any single sultan. He issues decrees in his own name from within it, dismisses and appoints ministers — the fall of the powerful vizier Ibn Shukr is laid at his door — and learns to rule not as a soldier holding a camp but as a prince holding a capital. The citadel will stand through every dynasty that follows the Ayyubids; it is the one monument of this reign that needs no treaty to survive.
suggested_refs: The Cairo Citadel (Qal'at al-Jabal), still crowning the city today

stops.name: Cairo, the Kamiliyya founded for the traditionists
stops.campa: Amid the wars this sultan founds, in the Jamaliyya quarter of Cairo, the Madrasa al-Kamiliyya: a house given wholly to the study of the hadith, the sayings of the Prophet, the discipline the learned call dar al-hadith. It becomes within a generation the most respected school of traditionists in Egypt. He is a man, his own chroniclers say, who loves the company of scholars more than the company of flatterers, who would rather argue a fine point of law or astronomy over a meal than be praised for victories he counts, in his own reckoning, as burdens rather than glories.
suggested_refs: The Madrasa al-Kamiliyya, Jamaliyya quarter, Cairo — founded 622 AH / 1225

stops.name: Damietta camp, the crown falls to him mid-siege
stops.campa: The Fifth Crusade's fleet has been anchored off Damietta since May, and in late August the crusaders storm the chain tower that bars the Nile, opening the river to their ships. Days later, in the field before the threatened city, word comes that al-Adil has died in Syria. Al-Kamil, already commanding Egypt's defense as viceroy, is now sultan in fact as well as name, inheriting a father's throne and a father's unfinished war in the same week, the crown descending on him between one assault and the next with no time allowed to mourn it.
suggested_refs: The chain tower of Damietta, key of the Nile, taken by the Crusaders 25 August 1218

stops.name: Damietta camp, the conspiracy of Ibn al-Mashtub
stops.campa: In the depth of the siege, with the army's confidence shaken, the amir Imad al-Din ibn al-Mashtub, commander of the Kurdish Hakkari regiment, conspires to unseat al-Kamil for his younger, more biddable brother al-Faiz. Warned in time, the sultan flees his own camp by night rather than face the plotters, and in the chaos the crusaders press their advantage and tighten their grip on Damietta. He considers, for a dark hour, sailing on to Yemen where his son already rules, and leaving Egypt to whoever can hold it, the nearest this reign comes to simply walking away from the throne.
suggested_refs: Ibn Wasil's account of the al-Mashtub conspiracy, Mufarrij al-Kurub
sources: Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub

stops.name: Damietta camp, al-Mu'azzam's ride, the conspiracy broken
stops.campa: His brother al-Mu'azzam Isa, lord of Damascus, rides down from Syria with reinforcements the moment word of the plot reaches him, and the conspiracy collapses as quickly as it rose: Ibn al-Mashtub is arrested and exiled, al-Faiz sent quietly home, the army made whole again around its rightful sultan. Al-Kamil returns to the siege lines a man twice tested in his first winter as ruler — once by the Franks outside the camp, once by his own captains within it — and twice, by his brother's loyalty, delivered.
suggested_refs: Al-Mu'azzam Isa of Damascus, whose march south saved his brother's throne
sources: Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub

stops.name: Fariskur, the first offer of Jerusalem
stops.campa: After a costly action near Fariskur, al-Kamil sends across the lines a proposal the crusader camp has not dared hope for: he will restore Jerusalem itself, rebuild what has been thrown down, return relics of the True Cross taken since Hattin, and grant a long truce, if only the army will leave Egypt in peace. His own captains think him mad to give away Salah al-Din's great prize so cheaply; he thinks the exchange plain arithmetic, a half-ruined city bought back against the granary of his kingdom. The legate Pelagius, certain of total victory, refuses to hear it.
suggested_refs: The Historia Damiatina of Oliver of Paderborn, recording the rejected offer

stops.name: Fariskur, the friar from Assisi
stops.campa: Two unarmed men are dragged into his tent crying Soldan, beaten and chained by soldiers who take them for spies: a small friar in a patched habit, Francesco of Assisi, and his companion Illuminato. Al-Kamil, expecting envoys or renegades, finds instead a man offering to walk into fire beside his own imams to prove which faith God favors. He will not light the fire, but he will not let the little man be harmed either. For days he keeps him near, listens to him preach without anger, offers gifts he refuses, and sends him back under armed escort, unconverted and unharmed, asking only a prayer in return.
stops.quote: Pray for me, that God may deign to reveal to me the law and the faith which is more pleasing to Him.
stops.quote_source: Jacques de Vitry, Historia occidentalis (the sultan's parting words to Francis, the earliest witness; retold in Bonaventure, Legenda Maior IX)
suggested_refs: Giotto, The Trial by Fire before the Sultan, Bardi Chapel, Santa Croce, Florence
saint_francis.journey.json — the Fariskur stop, the counter-shot to this one

stops.name: Damietta, the city falls, the dead in the streets
stops.campa: Damietta falls not to storm but to starvation: plague and famine have already emptied the city of half its people, and when the crusaders finally climb the undefended walls in the night they find streets carpeted with the dead, too weak even to be buried by the living who remain. Al-Kamil withdraws his broken army south to al-Mansurah rather than lose it entirely defending a corpse of a city. He has lost the greatest port of Egypt to a siege sixteen months long, and the offer of Jerusalem he made before its fall he does not withdraw; he repeats it, again and again, through the crusader winter to come.
suggested_refs: Oliver of Paderborn's Historia Damiatina on the fall of the city, 5 November 1219

stops.name: Jerusalem, the walls thrown down by his own brother
stops.campa: Fearing that a crusader army flush with Damietta might now strike at Jerusalem itself and hold it against every Ayyubid counter-siege, al-Mu'azzam Isa orders the walls of the Holy City thrown down with his own garrison's hands, the Dome of the Rock left standing amid rubble, the Franks denied a fortress even if they take the ground. Al-Kamil, still repeating his offer of the city to the enemy camp, watches his brother unmake by demolition what he is trying to give away by treaty, the two Ayyubid strategies, cession and destruction, arriving at the same conclusion: that Jerusalem, undefended, is worth less as a possession than as a gift withheld.
suggested_refs: The dismantled Ayyubid walls of Jerusalem, razed by al-Mu'azzam 1219-1220
sources: Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub

stops.name: Al-Mansurah, the sultan regroups, the offer renewed
stops.campa: At al-Mansurah, a new town he raises on the Nile above Damietta expressly to bar the road to Cairo, al-Kamil rebuilds his army through a slow year of standoff. Embassies pass back and forth across the lines; the sultan repeats his terms — Jerusalem, the True Cross, a lasting truce — to a crusader camp that is itself split, its soldiers and many of its knights eager to accept, its legate Pelagius and the arriving Italians still holding out for the full conquest of Egypt that a promised army under the Emperor Frederick has not yet sent. Al-Kamil waits, fortifies, and does not attack; he has learned that Egypt's flood is a weapon he need only leave loaded.
suggested_refs: The town of al-Mansurah, founded by al-Kamil as the new bar against Cairo

stops.name: Al-Mansurah, the crusaders march on Cairo
stops.campa: Against al-Kamil's terms and against the counsel of his own field commander John of Brienne, Pelagius orders the army south from Damietta toward Cairo itself, certain that one more push completes the conquest Damietta began. Al-Kamil falls back before them without a major battle, ceding ground he has no intention of holding, watching the crusader host advance deeper into the Delta between the branching arms of the Nile, into the exact country, flat and canal-cut and floodable, that he and his engineers have spent two years quietly preparing.
suggested_refs: The Delta floodplain between Damietta and al-Mansurah, the ground al-Kamil chose

stops.name: The Nile dams opened, the trap closes
stops.campa: With the crusader army strung out on the narrow ground between the Nile and the Bahr al-Saghir canal, al-Kamil gives the order his engineers have waited two years to carry out: the dams and sluices upstream are opened, and the annual Nile flood, already swollen, pours into the canals around the Frankish camp. Within days the ground the crusaders stand on has become an island, their supply lines to Damietta cut, their siege engines and horses mired, retreat itself impossible without ships he has already moved to block the river. No battle is fought; the river alone does what two years of siegecraft could not.
suggested_refs: The Bahr al-Saghir canal, whose flooding trapped the crusader army

stops.name: Al-Mansurah, the crusader surrender
stops.campa: Starving, flooded, and surrounded, Pelagius and John of Brienne sue for terms they refused two years running. Al-Kamil, holding every advantage, does not humiliate them: he offers the same bargain in reverse. The terms are an eight-year truce and the return of Damietta and every prisoner, in exchange for the crusader army's unmolested evacuation of Egypt. He feeds the starving Franks from his own stores before they march out. Oliver of Paderborn, who watched Christian soldiers die of hunger within sight of the sultan's provisions, will write plainly of the mercy shown a beaten enemy.
stops.quote: Who could doubt that such goodness, friendship and charity come from God? Men whose parents, sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, had died in agony at our hands, whose lands we took, whom we drove naked from their homes, revived us with their own food when we were dying of hunger and showered us with kindness even when we were in their power.
stops.quote_source: Oliver of Paderborn, Historia Damiatina, on al-Kamil's provisioning of the surrendered army
suggested_refs: Oliver of Paderborn's testimony to al-Kamil's clemency at the surrender

stops.name: Damietta restored, the truce of eight years
stops.campa: The crusader army marches out of Egypt and Damietta is handed back on the eighth of September, exactly the terms al-Kamil offered before the city ever fell in the first place, now bought back at the cost of a war that gained the Franks nothing they did not already have. He rides into the recovered port at the head of his own household, the True Cross among the returned relics, the Fifth Crusade ended not by a decisive battle but by a river he chose the hour to release. Egypt is his again, whole; the offer he made and was refused three times has cost his enemies everything and himself almost nothing.
suggested_refs: The Journal / chronicle record of the Damietta handover, September 1221

stops.name: Cairo, trade with Venice and the works of peace
stops.campa: With the Franks gone from Egyptian soil, al-Kamil turns to the labor he prefers to war: he renews and extends trade agreements with Venice and the other Italian maritime cities, opening Alexandria and Damietta again to the merchants whose galleys had lately carried an invading army. Customs revenue rebuilds a treasury drained by three years of siege; canals and dikes broken in the flood he himself unleashed are repaired; the same engineering that trapped an army now waters the fields that feed it. He governs, his own court remembers, as a man more interested in the welfare of the ruled than in the glory of the ruler.
suggested_refs: The Venetian trading quarter of Alexandria, reopened under al-Kamil's peace

stops.name: Damascus, the rift with al-Mu'azzam over strategy
stops.campa: The brother who saved his throne before Damietta becomes, in peace, his rival: al-Mu'azzam of Damascus resents al-Kamil's willingness to trade land for treaties and courts the sultan's enemies in turn, even flirting with alliance against Egypt's dealings with the Franks and, more dangerously, with the Khwarazmian adventurer Jalal al-Din to the east. The house of Ayyub, never more than a confederation of cousins under a single eldest claim, strains again along its oldest fault line, the same rivalry between Cairo and Damascus that split Saladin's own sons a generation before. Al-Kamil, watching, begins to draw his youngest brother al-Ashraf of the Jazira toward Egypt's side of the quarrel.
suggested_refs: The rival Ayyubid courts of Cairo and Damascus, never fully reconciled

stops.name: Damascus, the death of al-Mu'azzam opens the door
stops.campa: Al-Mu'azzam dies in Damascus, leaving Syria and Palestine to his young son al-Nasir Dawud, a nephew with neither his father's army nor his standing among the family's elders. The rivalry that shadowed al-Kamil's decade of peace is broken at a stroke; he and al-Ashraf, closing ranks against the inexperienced heir, begin to plan the recovery of Damascus for the elder branch of the house. It is this quarrel over the nephew's inheritance, more than any crusader army, that will decide the fate of Jerusalem in the two years to come, a city about to be handed twice over as small change in a family settlement.
suggested_refs: The tomb of al-Mu'azzam Isa in Damascus, whose death reopened the succession

stops.name: Cairo, Fakhr al-Din sent to Sicily
stops.campa: Needing a counterweight against his brother al-Mu'azzam while the Damascus quarrel still burns, al-Kamil opens correspondence with an unlikely partner: Frederick II Hohenstaufen, Holy Roman Emperor and King of Sicily, sends embassies proposing an alliance, and al-Kamil answers in kind, dispatching his trusted emir Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh to the Sicilian court to treat directly with a Christian ruler raised among Arabic tutors and known already for his taste in Muslim learning. The sultan is playing a game two moves deep: a German army arriving as his ally against Damascus is worth infinitely more to him than the same army arriving as an enemy at Damietta again.
suggested_refs: Fakhr al-Din ibn al-Shaykh, the emir who shuttled between Cairo and Sicily 1226-1229
sources: medievalists.net, 'Frederick II and Islam: Separating Myth from Reality'

stops.name: Cairo, the emperor's questions on the heavens
stops.campa: Between the clauses of alliance, Frederick sends al-Kamil something no crusader king has sent before: questions of philosophy and natural science, on the eternity of the world, the nature of the soul, the working of the heavens, put to the sultan's scholars as one court of learning to another. Al-Kamil, who founded a madrasa for the study of tradition and loves nothing better than an evening's disputation, answers with evident pleasure, setting his own philosophers and astronomers to the emperor's puzzles. It is, on both sides, a genuine exchange of minds conducted in the pauses of a war neither man especially wants to finish fighting.
suggested_refs: The correspondence on philosophy and science between al-Kamil's court and Frederick II
sources: researchgate.net, 'Sultan al-Kamil, Emperor Frederick II and the Submission of Jerusalem'

stops.name: Cairo, the gift of the sphere of stars
stops.campa: Among the gifts that pass between the two courts through Fakhr al-Din's hands, one becomes legend on both sides of the sea: a tent pierced through with small holes, so that a lamp lit within casts the pattern of the stars and planets across its own dark ceiling, a portable heaven a prince can carry to camp. Al-Kamil, whose interest in astronomy is no courtly affectation, sends it as a token between minds that understand each other better across the space of an ocean and a faith than either does with half his own barons, a fitting emblem of a friendship built entirely on parchment and never once on a shared table.
suggested_refs: The star-tent given to Frederick II, an early planetarium, recorded in the chronicles of his court
sources: researchgate.net, 'Sultan al-Kamil, Emperor Frederick II and the Submission of Jerusalem'

stops.name: Near Acre, Frederick's fleet arrives, an excommunicate crusader
stops.campa: Frederick lands at last on the Syrian coast, two years late by the pope's reckoning and excommunicated for the delay, commanding a crusade the Church itself refuses to bless. He comes not to conquer but to collect the debt al-Kamil's own diplomacy has been building for two years, and finds the debt has changed shape beneath him: al-Mu'azzam is dead, the alliance against Damascus al-Kamil originally wanted no longer needs Frederick's sword, only his name and his patience at the negotiating table while Fakhr al-Din works out what an emperor with no real army behind him can still be given in exchange for going home satisfied.
suggested_refs: Frederick II's landing at Acre, 7 September 1228, opening the Sixth Crusade

stops.name: Tall al-Ajul, the camp above Gaza, the real war to the north
stops.campa: He has sat since November on the old mound above the Wadi Ghazza, the army of Egypt tented around him, while Frederick waits at Jaffa a day's ride up the coast. From here he runs two wars at once: the emperor's envoys coming in over the dunes, and to the north his brother al-Ashraf opening the attack on Damascus, where their young nephew al-Nasir Dawud holds the city his father left him. The timing is no accident. A settled peace over half-ruined Jerusalem, a city he has already watched his own brother demolish, frees every soldier he has for the prize he actually wants.
suggested_refs: Tall al-Ajul on the Wadi Ghazza, al-Kamil's camp from November 1228 to late April 1229
The walls of Damascus, the true object of al-Kamil's 1229 campaign

stops.name: Tall al-Ajul, the Treaty of Jaffa sealed through Fakhr al-Din
stops.campa: The two rulers never meet; the treaty that ends the Sixth Crusade is carried between two camps by emissaries, Fakhr al-Din for al-Kamil, Thomas of Aquino and Balian of Sidon for Frederick, a draft on the eleventh, the sealed thing on the eighteenth. Jerusalem passes to the emperor with a corridor to the coast, Bethlehem and Nazareth besides, for a truce of ten years, five months and forty days; but the Haram al-Sharif stays under Muslim law, a Muslim garrison and a Muslim qadi, the call to prayer sounding as it always has. He has traded a city he cannot defend for a decade to finish his real war.
stops.quote: We have only conceded to them some churches and some ruined houses. The sacred precincts, the venerated Rock and all the other sanctuaries... remain ours as they have always been.
stops.quote_source: Al-Kamil's own justification of the treaty, as reported by Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Jaffa, 18 February 1229, negotiated wholly by intermediaries
sources: Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub

stops.name: Jerusalem, Frederick crowns himself, word reaches the sultan
stops.campa: Frederick enters the demolished, ungarrisoned city on the seventeenth of March, escorted by Shams al-Din, the qadi of Nablus, and the next day — excommunicate, unblessed by any bishop willing to touch him — crowns himself in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre with his own hands. Word of it reaches al-Kamil's camp at Tall al-Ajul within days, and with it a stranger report: that the qadi, out of esteem for his guest, had ordered the muezzins of the sacred precinct not to give the call that night, and that the emperor, learning of it in the morning, rebuked him for the courtesy.
stops.quote: You committed an error in what you did. By God, the greatest of my aims in staying overnight in Jerusalem was to hear the muezzins making the call to prayer and glorifying God in the night.
stops.quote_source: Frederick II to the qadi Shams al-Din, as reported by Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub
suggested_refs: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where Frederick crowned himself 18 March 1229
Ibn Wasil's account of the muezzin anecdote, reported to al-Kamil's court
sources: Ibn Wasil, Mufarrij al-Kurub fi Akhbar Bani Ayyub

stops.name: Damascus, the sermon against the treaty
stops.campa: In the great Umayyad Mosque, while the city braces for his uncle's siege, the preacher Sibt ibn al-Jawzi mounts the pulpit at al-Nasir Dawud's own command and denounces the surrender of Jerusalem in words that cross the Muslim world faster than any treaty clause: how, he asks the weeping congregation, can the son of al-Adil hand back in an afternoon of parchment what Salah al-Din's sword took forty years to win? The sermon is a weapon of the siege as much as any mangonel. Al-Kamil, who counts the bargain shrewd, absorbs the charge of treachery without answering it in kind.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus, pulpit of Sibt ibn al-Jawzi's condemnation
sources: Sibt ibn al-Jawzi, Mir'at al-Zaman (as summarized in secondary scholarship)

stops.name: Damascus, the siege completed, the city surrenders to al-Ashraf
stops.campa: Freed by the Jaffa settlement to press the real campaign, al-Kamil and al-Ashraf close the ring around Damascus; after two months of hard fighting the city surrenders on the twenty-fifth of June, and al-Nasir Dawud is bought off with Transjordan and the fortress of Kerak in place of the capital his father left him. Al-Kamil gives Damascus itself to al-Ashraf rather than take it for Egypt, content, as he has always been, to hold the balance of the family rather than swallow it whole, the same instinct that traded away Jerusalem now redistributing Syria without a drop more blood than the siege required.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Damascus, surrendered 25 June 1229 and given to al-Ashraf

stops.name: Cairo, the arbiter of the house governs on
stops.campa: With Damascus settled on al-Ashraf and Jerusalem on a ten-year lease to an emperor who has already sailed home, al-Kamil returns to the work he prefers above all others: the government of Egypt, the courts, the canals, the endowments to scholars and traditionists, correspondence with Frederick continuing across the years in matters of philosophy long after the treaty that occasioned it is signed. He is, by now, the oldest and most experienced ruler in the Islamic Mediterranean, the eldest of Salah al-Din's nephews still holding real power, presiding over a peace between Cairo, Damascus and the Franks that no one thought could last this long, and that only he, among his own family, seems to have wanted.
suggested_refs: The diwan of Cairo in al-Kamil's final decade of rule

stops.name: The Jazira frontier, the Khwarazmian threat gathers
stops.campa: In the east a new and far less courteous power presses on the Ayyubid marches: Jalal al-Din Mingburnu, the last Khwarazmshah, fleeing the Mongols, carves a bloody path through Ayyubid Armenia and Jazira territory, sacking towns his own family once counted as allies. Al-Kamil, who spent a decade trading cities for peace with Christian kings, finds no such bargain possible with the Khwarazmian; he joins a coalition of Ayyubid and Seljuk rulers against him, the diplomat's long patience finally exhausted by an enemy who wants only the ground beneath his feet and nothing that can be negotiated for.
suggested_refs: The Ayyubid-Seljuk coalition against Jalal al-Din, formed under al-Kamil's later reign

stops.name: Amid, the black city on the Tigris taken
stops.campa: The Artuqid lords have held Diyar Bakr since before Salah al-Din's day. Al-Kamil brings the combined Ayyubid armies and their vassals against them, and on the eighteenth of October al-Mas'ud surrenders Amid, the black basalt city walled above the Tigris; Hisn Kayfa, held out for a month more, falls in November. The sultan who gave Jerusalem away without a battle takes an eastern principality by siege, and hands it entire to his son as-Salih Ayyub, twenty-seven years old. The house is enlarged eastward and, in the same stroke, quietly divided against itself.
suggested_refs: The basalt walls of Amid (Diyarbakir), surrendered to al-Kamil 18 October 1232
Hisn Kayfa (Hasankeyf) on the Tigris, taken November 1232

stops.name: Harran, beaten by the Seljuk in the north
stops.campa: Alarmed at the Seljuk sultan Kayqubad swelling across eastern Anatolia, al-Kamil leads a coalition of Ayyubid princes north, takes Kharput on the upper Euphrates, and is then beaten outright. Kayqubad routs the allied armies and comes on southward, taking Siverek, Urfa, Harran and Raqqa, the very marches al-Kamil first campaigned in as a young man of nineteen. It is the plainest military defeat of his reign, suffered not against Franks but against a fellow Muslim sovereign. He recovers Urfa within four months and then does what he has always done in the end: sends envoys, until the frontier is talked back toward quiet.
suggested_refs: Harran, lost to Kayqubad I in the counteroffensive of 1234

stops.name: Damascus, al-Ashraf dies and the city is closed to him
stops.campa: Al-Ashraf, the brother who stood beside him for thirty years, dies in Damascus in August, and their younger brother as-Salih Ismail takes the city without waiting on the sultan's word. Al-Kamil brings his army north in October and finds his own lessons turned against him: Ismail burns and levels the suburbs of Damascus so that no Egyptian soldier can shelter or forage in them, and the siege stalls in the cold with nothing gained. For the first time in twenty years the arbiter of the house of Ayyub is refused by the house itself.
suggested_refs: The razed suburbs of Damascus, denied to al-Kamil's army in the failed siege of 1237
sources: kurdish-history.com, 'The Complex Rule of Al-Malik al-Salih Ismail'

stops.name: Damascus, the two crowns held at last
stops.campa: He returns in the new year and this time the city opens to him. As-Salih Ismail is bought out with Baalbek and Bosra rather than broken, in the old manner, and al-Kamil enters Damascus as its sultan as well as Egypt's, the two crowns of the Ayyubid world gathered, for the first and only time in his life, into one pair of hands. He is fifty-eight or sixty depending which chronicler is counting, and he has spent forty years arguing that the house entire is worth more than any single city of it. He will hold the proof nine weeks.
suggested_refs: The citadel of Damascus, entered by al-Kamil as sultan in January 1238

stops.name: Damascus, illness and the sultan's death
stops.campa: Nine weeks after the gates opened to him the illnesses close in together — a cough, a flux of the bowels, the old gout in his legs — and the sultan is carried to a small room of the Dar al-Qasaba inside the citadel. It is the room where his uncle Salah al-Din died forty-five years before. He has outlived Saladin's whole generation, outlived al-Mu'azzam and al-Ashraf both, turned back both crusades that came at Egypt on terms mostly his own. No enemy stands over the bed; it is the exhaustion of long rule that takes him, on a Thursday night, in his sixtieth year.

stops.name: Damascus, burial, and the house of Ayyub unravels
stops.campa: He is buried the next day inside the citadel where he died, amid the mourning of a dynasty that, within days, resumes the quarrel he spent his reign suppressing: his sons as-Salih Ayyub in the east and al-Adil II in Cairo divide the inheritance he tried to keep whole, and the Ayyubid house slides back into the fratricidal politics of Saladin's own sons two generations before. The peace with the Franks he built stone by traded stone will outlive him barely a decade before the Mamluks he first brought to Egypt as slave-soldiers take the sultanate from his line, but for twenty years, a war-torn coast knew, because of him, more truce than battle.
